title: Running a Minecraft server inside GitHub Codespaces
body:
GitHub Codespaces is a cloud development environment. You get a container, a browser-based VS Code, and a public URL for port forwarding. It is absolutely not meant to host game servers.

So naturally I used it to host a modded Minecraft 1.16.5 server.

The approach was straightforward in theory: install Java inside the container, drop in a Forge server JAR, use Ngrok to expose the port, share the address. In practice there were about four layers of port-forwarding nonsense and a DNS issue that took longer to debug than the whole rest of the setup. Codespaces has its own internal networking rules and Ngrok had opinions about tunneling game traffic.

But it worked. Friends joined from three countries. The server ran modded 1.16.5 with a dozen mods including Create, which felt appropriate — a factory mod running inside a GitHub container inside a browser. I poured a lot of hours into that world before they patched it.

The lesson is not 'here is how to run Minecraft on Codespaces' — they have since closed that door. The lesson is that most infrastructure constraints are softer than they look, and curiosity plus an afternoon is usually enough to find the edge.

title: What building a 6D Kalman filter taught me about knowing when to stop
body:
Most trajectory tracking tutorials use a 4D Kalman filter: two position dimensions, two velocity dimensions. The standard advice is that this is enough.

I disagreed, for a specific reason. A volleyball in flight is under gravity, and gravity is constant and known. If you model acceleration as a state variable instead of noise, your predictions during occlusion — when the ball disappears behind a player or goes out of frame — get dramatically smoother. You are not guessing anymore, you are integrating a known physical law.

So I built a 6D filter: x, y, vx, vy, ax, ay. This part was honestly not that hard. The math is well-documented. What was hard was the detection layer feeding into the filter.

I was fusing three independent detectors: color-based (HSV thresholding on the ball's color), shape-based (Hough circle transform), and motion-based (frame differencing). Each detector has different failure modes. Color fails in bad lighting. Shape fails when the ball is partially occluded. Motion fails when the ball is stationary relative to the camera.

Getting three disagreeing detectors to produce one confident detection — without just averaging them and hoping — took most of the project time. The filter itself was two days of work. The fusion logic was three weeks.

The thing I keep thinking about: at some point I had a system that worked well enough. It tracked the ball through most occluions, kept decent predictions, ran at acceptable FPS. The temptation was to keep going — add a fourth detector, retrain on more data, tune the noise covariance matrices further. I made myself stop and document instead.

Finished is better than optimal. I have not always believed this.

title: Why I still run Arch in 2025
body:
People ask me this with the tone of someone asking why you still take the bus when cars exist.

The honest answer: I learn more fixing a broken Arch install at 2AM than I do in a week of coursework. Not because I enjoy suffering — I do not enjoy suffering — but because when something breaks on Arch, you have to understand what actually happened. There is no 'click repair' button. There is a log file, a forum thread from 2019 that is almost relevant, and you.

I have rebuilt my system from a broken bootloader twice. I have had a kernel update kill my display manager and had to recover from a TTY. I once misconfigured PAM and locked myself out of sudo, which is a special kind of problem. Every one of these events taught me something I could not have learned from a tutorial.

The AUR is also genuinely unmatched. The packaging ecosystem on Arch is the closest thing Linux has to 'it just works for obscure software.'

I should say: I do not think Arch is for everyone. If you want a machine that runs reliably and you do not particularly want to understand why, use something else. Ubuntu is fine. Fedora is great. The point of Arch is not that it is better — the point is that it costs you something, and what you pay in time you receive in understanding.

I run a riced Void setup as my secondary. Void is Arch with fewer opinions and a better init system. The ricing is a separate hobby that I am slightly embarrassed about the hours I have put into it.

title: logscope: I built a SIEM because I wanted one
body:
The origin of logscope is embarrassingly simple: I was doing log analysis work at Royal Air Maroc, parsing auth logs manually with grep and awk, and I thought — there should be a tool for this that does not require a $40,000 enterprise license or a cloud dependency.

So I built one.

logscope is a lightweight SIEM for local Linux log monitoring. It parses /var/log/auth.log, /var/log/syslog, /var/log/kern.log, and their RHEL equivalents. It detects SSH brute-force attempts, root logins, off-hours access, port scans inferred from firewall DROP patterns, new user creation, and a handful of other things that should make you look twice. Every finding gets a severity score: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL. The output is a colored terminal report via rich, or JSON if you want to pipe it somewhere.

The most interesting design decision was the severity escalation logic. A successful SSH login is LOW by default. But if it happens at 3AM, it escalates to HIGH. If it happens as root at 3AM, it becomes CRITICAL. Context changes meaning — that felt important to encode properly rather than just flagging everything as the same severity.

It has a --demo flag that runs against synthetic log data, so you can see what it does without needing a server with actual incidents on it. That flag took longer than it should have to build because I wanted the demo data to look realistic rather than obviously fake.

The project is on GitHub. It is not enterprise software and I am not pretending it is. But it runs, it finds real things, and it cost nothing to deploy.

title: On wanting to be somewhere else
body:
I have wanted to live in Norway since my second year of university. Not as an escape — or not only as an escape — but because something about the way Norwegians seem to approach life maps onto something I cannot fully articulate about what I want from my own.

Work as a thing you do for part of the day, not your whole identity. Nature as a daily presence, not a weekend trip. A country small enough that institutions are accountable, large enough that interesting things happen. The word friluftsliv — open-air life — which does not translate cleanly into English because English does not quite have the concept.

I was ready to apply to the University of Oslo in year two. My parents said no — they had invested in an American degree, and an American degree was what made sense. They were not wrong about the credential. They were right in the way that practical people are right about practical things.

Now it is year four and the US has changed enough that the plan that made sense then makes less sense now. So Norway is back on the table. I am learning the language — slowly, on Duolingo, which feels insufficient and is probably insufficient, but it is a start. I am targeting Norwegian security companies. I am trying to figure out how to become someone a Norwegian employer would take seriously before I arrive.

I do not know if it will work. I know I have wanted it long enough that it is worth trying seriously rather than just dreaming about. That is about as much certainty as I have right now, and I am learning to treat that as enough.

title: M.T.A.: building a robot because I miss making things
body:
I bought a 3D printer this morning. Not after months of research — I woke up, had breakfast, and ordered one. The project that justified it has been sitting in my head for over a year.

M.T.A. stands for Mobile Travel Assistant. The concept: a desktop companion robot that can also move. Tank treads for rough terrain. A warm personality — think BMO from Adventure Time, that specific energy of something small and functional that also has feelings about things. A Raspberry Pi 4B for the brain. TTS and speech recognition so it can talk back. A camera so it can see the room.

The LLM is the interesting part. Running a capable language model locally on a Pi is not realistic — too slow, too resource-hungry. My solution: host the model on my local server and have the Pi communicate with it over the home network. There is some latency. That is fine. BMO does not need to respond in milliseconds. BMO needs to respond with personality.

I already have the 3D models. I already have the Pi set up with a working personality — the TTS is running, the speech recognition works, the server-side LLM is responding. What I did not have was the physical shell. That is what the printer is for.

I have been playing Satisfactory for years. Thousands of hours. The thing I love about that game is not the optimization — it is the moment when the factory is running and something you designed is producing something useful. I want that feeling in physical space.

M.T.A. is probably not going to change anything. It is not a product. It is not a startup idea. It is a thing I want to exist in my room, built by my hands, that talks back when I talk to it. That feels like enough of a reason.
